passage: Behind the panchayat school, Jagdish snatched the clay bullock from Preeti's hands and it snapped at the horn. Preeti's face crumpled. Their teacher, Meena Didi, came over. “Say sorry, Jagdish.” He mumbled “sorry” to the ground and turned away. Preeti stood holding the broken horn, sniffing. Jagdish glanced back at her wet cheeks, hesitated, then fetched a wet rag and a dab of mud from the water pot. He pressed the horn back on. “I can stick it,” he said quietly.

qa.q: What snapped when Jagdish snatched the clay bullock?
qa.a: The clay bullock snapped at the horn.

qa.q: What might Jagdish have been feeling when he came back with the wet rag, and what else could explain it?
qa.a: Probably he saw Preeti's wet cheeks and felt bad, wanting to fix what he broke, since he glanced back at her first. Another reading is that he wanted to avoid more trouble with the teacher.

qa.q: What could Meena Didi do next so the sorry means more?
qa.a: She could point out that he noticed Preeti's hurt and tried to mend it, and let the two of them finish fixing the bullock together.

qa.q: How might Preeti see the mumbled sorry compared with the mending?
qa.a: The mumbled sorry to the ground may have felt empty, while the mending shows someone cared about her broken bullock, so she may feel better.

grounding: A prompted, mumbled sorry is only a start; the child sees the hurt and helps repair it.

passage: “Sorry,” said Xin, loudly, because his mother was standing at the sandpit gate. Nadia, whose sandcastle he had just stepped on, kept her eyes on the flattened heap. “Say it nicely,” his mother said. “I said it,” Xin muttered, and the two of them stood there. Then Xin knelt, scooped damp sand with both hands and began piling it back into a mound. He stopped and looked at her. “Where does the tower go?” Nadia sniffed, pointed, and handed him the little bucket.

qa.q: Whose sandcastle did Xin step on?
qa.a: He stepped on Nadia's sandcastle.

qa.q: What was Xin probably feeling when he asked where the tower goes, and what else could it be?
qa.a: Probably he felt sorry once he saw the flattened heap and wanted to help, since he knelt and rebuilt the mound. He might also have wanted to end the awkward standing around.

qa.q: What small step would help Xin's mother support him next time?
qa.a: She could give him a moment before prompting, and later say something like “you helped build it back” instead of pressing for the word again.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Nadia when Xin first said sorry?
qa.a: She kept her eyes on the flattened heap, so the word may have done little because her castle was still broken. When he helped rebuild, she pointed and handed him the bucket, which suggests she felt included again.

grounding: The forced sorry is a start; real apology grows when Xin sees the hurt and helps repair it.

passage: Deepika's aunt clapped when she finished the rhyme at the Sunday gathering in the flat. “Wah! Again, again!” Deepika's hands flew to her face and she giggled through her fingers, rocking on her heels. Her friend Farida from downstairs watched from the sofa arm. Deepika peeked out, ducked back, then hurried behind the curtain, still giggling. After a minute Farida's mother said, “Nobody has to do it again,” and the clapping stopped. Deepika slid out and sat beside Farida.

qa.q: What did Deepika do when her aunt clapped for the rhyme?
qa.a: Her hands flew to her face and she giggled through her fingers.

qa.q: What might Deepika have been feeling behind the curtain, and what else could it be?
qa.a: Likely shy and embarrassed at suddenly being the centre of attention, though pleased too, since she kept giggling and peeking out. It could also be plain excitement and a wish for a game of hide and seek.

qa.q: What could the grown-ups do to make her comfortable?
qa.a: They could praise her quietly and later in private, and not push her to perform again, as Farida's mother did by saying nobody had to.

qa.q: How might Farida see Deepika's hiding?
qa.a: Farida watched from the sofa arm and may have found it funny or just seen shyness. Deepika sitting beside her afterwards suggests Farida felt like a safe friend. 🙂

grounding: Embarrassment shows as covering the face and nervous giggling; quiet handling helps.

passage:
“Parul Ma'am says you counted to fifty all alone today!” said Mummy.
“Nooo,” said Vasudha, dragging her dupatta over her head. “Who told?”
“Parul Ma'am did.”
Vasudha giggled and hid her face in the cushion. “Don't say it loud.”
“All right, only a whisper.” Mummy leaned close. “Fifty,” she whispered.
Vasudha peeked out, cheeks pink. “I skipped forty-four.”
“Did you? Shall we count again together?”
“Okay. But you close your eyes.”

qa.q: Which number did Vasudha say she skipped?
qa.a: She said she skipped forty-four.

qa.q: Why did Vasudha hide her face in the cushion, and what else could explain it?
qa.a: Being praised made her shy and embarrassed, and she asked Mummy not to say it loud. It could also mean she was pleased and a little proud but not ready to show it.

qa.q: Which choice by Mummy worked, and why?
qa.a: She whispered the praise, so it stayed private and Vasudha felt safe enough to peek out and talk about her counting. She could later ask to hear the counting again in a quiet moment.

qa.q: How might Mummy see Vasudha's hiding?
qa.a: She may see it as sweet shyness, a sign Vasudha cares what others think, so she lowers her voice instead of teasing.

grounding: A preschooler hides her face when her achievement is noticed; private, kind handling helps.

passage: Javier tripped on the playground gravel and sat there, lip trembling, knees stinging, tears starting. Rafael, who had been rolling a red toy truck along the wall, stopped. He walked over, looked at Javier's face, and pushed the truck across the gravel to him. When Javier kept crying, Rafael put an arm halfway around his shoulders and patted twice; Javier leaned toward him. Their teacher, Ms Ortiz, crouched nearby. “Rafael, you gave Javier your truck. You saw he was sad and wanted to help.” Rafael nodded and looked at the truck.

qa.q: What toy did Rafael push across the gravel to Javier?
qa.a: He pushed a red toy truck across the gravel.

qa.q: What did Rafael want when he pushed the truck over and patted Javier?
qa.a: He wanted to make Javier feel better; he saw the sad face and gave something he liked. It is a simple offer, and he may also have just wanted the crying to stop.

qa.q: How could Ms Ortiz's words help Rafael learn?
qa.a: By naming that he saw Javier was sad and wanted to help, she links the feeling to the caring act. She could also ask Javier what he would like.

qa.q: How might Javier feel about the truck and the pat?
qa.a: He may feel comforted that someone noticed, though his knees still sting and a truck may not be what he wanted. Leaning toward Rafael is the clue that the closeness was welcome. 🤍

grounding: Early sympathy: a child offers a toy and a pat to a crying friend, and an adult names it.

passage: During free play at the community centre creche, Darshan started crying loudly when his mother waved goodbye at the door and left for work. Urmila, at the block table, stared at him. She picked up her stuffed elephant and held it out. “This is Bholu. He can sit with you.” Darshan pushed it away, still crying. Urmila frowned, then sat down beside him without a word and kept Bholu on her own lap, patting his head. Caregiver Sunita noticed. “Urmila, you stayed with him. That is kind.”

qa.q: What did Urmila offer Darshan?
qa.a: She offered her stuffed elephant, Bholu.

qa.q: What was Urmila feeling when Darshan pushed the elephant away, and what else might it mean?
qa.a: Probably confused or a little disappointed but still wanting to comfort him, since she sat down beside him. It could also be that she was unsure what to do and staying was easiest.

qa.q: How could Sunita build on this moment?
qa.a: She could keep naming what Urmila did, and gently tell her that Darshan may want quiet company more than a toy right now.

qa.q: What is it like for Darshan when the toy is offered?
qa.a: He is missing his mother, so an elephant may not fix it, and pushing it away does not mean he disliked Urmila's offer. Her quiet sitting beside him may feel safer.

grounding: A young child offers a toy and stays near a crying friend; the adult names it.

passage: Mridul here, writing about my little cousin Eshaan, who is five. Yesterday I watched him at the window with his cup of milk when it started to hail. He stopped mid-sip, tilted his head and frowned. “Huh? It's raining ice?” He held out his hand and caught a piece of ice, then stared as it vanished. I couldn't tell if he was scared or just thinking. I said, “It's frozen rain.” He nodded slowly, then put another piece in the sink to watch.

qa.q: What did Eshaan catch in his hand?
qa.a: He caught a piece of ice in his hand.

qa.q: What was Eshaan most likely feeling when he tilted his head and frowned, and what else could it be?
qa.a: Most likely puzzled, because ice falling did not fit what he knew about rain, and he said “Huh?”. Mridul could not be sure, so he might also have been a little scared.

qa.q: How could Mridul help Eshaan with his puzzlement?
qa.a: Explain simply that it is frozen rain, then let him try his own ideas, like watching a piece melt in the sink.

qa.q: Why might Mridul find it hard to read Eshaan's face?
qa.a: A frown and a tilted head can show worry or thinking, and Eshaan did not say which. Mridul admits not knowing if he was scared.

grounding: A preschooler tilts head, frowns and says huh when something does not fit; simple explanation and trying ideas follow.

passage:
Monday: Madhuri turned a round moon piece over the sun-shaped hole. She tilted her head and frowned. “Huh?” Gurpreet Sir waited. “Doesn't fit,” she said, and gave up.
Wednesday: on the playground she stared at her shadow. “Huh? Why is it stuck to me?” Gurpreet Sir asked, “What do you think?” She shrugged and ran to see if it would come off.
Friday: in the dim room with the torch, she held up her hand and watched the wall, stepping close and back. “It gets big when I go near the light!” she said, and tried it again.

qa.q: What did Madhuri stare at on Wednesday?
qa.a: She stared at her shadow on the playground.

qa.q: What was Madhuri feeling on Monday when she said “Huh?”, and what else could it be?
qa.a: Puzzled, since the round moon piece would not fit the sun-shaped hole and she tilted her head and frowned. Giving up could also mean she was a bit frustrated or bored.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet Sir do that let Madhuri's thinking grow?
qa.a: He waited and asked what she thought instead of giving the answer, so by Friday she was trying ideas with the torch herself.

qa.q: What would change if Gurpreet Sir had explained shadows on Wednesday?
qa.a: She might have had the fact sooner but less chance to test her own ideas, though some children would also need a short explanation.

grounding: A puzzled preschooler is given room to try ideas over several days.

passage:
Paulo pressed his nose against the kitchen window while rain ran down the glass. “Why does it fall down?”
Soo-ah, his mother, was chopping scallions. “The earth pulls things down.”
“Why?”
“Good question. I'm not sure how to say it. Shall we look it up after dinner?”
“Why do we look it up?”
“Because books know more than I do about that.”
He considered this, dropped a toy car off the sill and watched it fall. “It's pulled,” he said.

qa.q: What was Soo-ah chopping?
qa.a: She was chopping scallions.

qa.q: What does Paulo dropping the toy car suggest he was thinking?
qa.a: That he was testing the idea that things get pulled down, so his questions come from real thinking. It could also be that he simply liked dropping things.

qa.q: What would you advise Soo-ah when her answers run out?
qa.a: Do what she did: say honestly that she is not sure and offer to look it up together, so he learns that questions have places to be answered.

qa.q: How might Soo-ah feel when the whys keep coming?
qa.a: She may enjoy his curiosity but feel stretched while cooking, and she seems comfortable admitting she is not sure. 🙂

grounding: A young child asks why about rain; an honest answer and a shared search build trust.

passage:
At circle time in the school's nursery section, Minakshi raised her hand before Bhavna Ma'am had finished the rule. “Walk, don't run in the corridor.”
“Why?”
“So nobody falls.”
“Why would they fall?”
“Floors can be slippery.”
“Why is the floor slippery?”
Another child sighed. Bhavna Ma'am smiled. “You ask a lot of whys, Minakshi. At lunch let's go and look at the floor together, and you tell me what you find.” Minakshi nodded, eyes on the corridor door.

qa.q: What rule did Bhavna Ma'am give at circle time?
qa.a: She said, “Walk, don't run in the corridor.”

qa.q: What might Minakshi be wanting when she keeps asking why?
qa.a: She wants to understand the reason behind the rule, and her eyes on the corridor door show she is already thinking about the floor. Another reading is that she enjoys getting the teacher's attention.

qa.q: How could Bhavna Ma'am handle many whys in a busy class?
qa.a: By promising a shared look at the floor at lunch, as she did, she gives Minakshi a real path to an answer without stalling the whole circle.

qa.q: How might another child feel about the whys?
qa.a: One child sighed, so some may feel impatient waiting for circle time to move on, while others may be curious too.

grounding: A young child's endless why about a rule shows thinking; a shared search follows.

passage: “Me first! Me first!” Nkechi shot up from the reading mat, arm stretched so high her shoulder shook. The teacher held up a paper star. “The star goes round the circle. When it reaches you, it's your turn.” Nkechi sat, hands squeezed between her knees, bouncing. Hana had the star first and passed it on. Nkechi watched each pair of hands it went through, lips pressed together. When it finally reached her, she took a big breath and began, “My dog...”

qa.q: What object went round the circle?
qa.a: A paper star went round the circle.

qa.q: What was Nkechi feeling while she waited for the star?
qa.a: Eager and excited to share, with some impatience: she bounced and pressed her lips together with her hands squeezed between her knees. She may also have worried her idea would be forgotten.

qa.q: How did the star rule help Nkechi?
qa.a: It gave a clear, fair signal for when her turn would come, so she had something concrete to watch while she waited.

qa.q: How might Hana see Nkechi's jumping up?
qa.a: Hana had the star first and may have felt watched or a little rushed by an eager friend, or she may simply have been excited too. Nothing in the scene says which.

grounding: Eagerness shows as jumping up and shouting me first; a turn-taking rule helps manage the wait.

passage:
“Who can tell me the colour of the sky?” asked Zainab Miss.
Rehana's hand shot up before the question ended. “Me, me, me first!” She hopped from foot to foot, then half stood, fingers wiggling.
“Rehana, I see your hand. Let's take two hands first, one at a time.”
Rehana sat down, but her arm stayed up, held at the wrist by her other hand. Two children answered. Then Zainab Miss said, “Rehana.”
“Blue... and grey when rain comes!” she burst out.

qa.q: What question did Zainab Miss ask?
qa.a: She asked, “Who can tell me the colour of the sky?”

qa.q: What does Rehana holding up her arm with her other hand suggest?
qa.a: She is eager to answer and trying to hold herself in during the wait. It could also hint at some nerves about being chosen.

qa.q: What small step helps eager children like Rehana wait?
qa.a: Saying that you see the raised hand and how many turns come first, as Zainab Miss did, so the wait has an end.

qa.q: What might the two children who answered first feel?
qa.a: Perhaps pleased to be chosen, or a bit rushed with Rehana hopping beside them. 🙂

grounding: Eager preschooler shouts me first; a clear turn rule helps.

passage:
The sky over the flat turned grey at eight, and the picnic bus left at nine. Arohi stood at the window in her sun hat, two fingers crossed. “I hope it doesn't rain, I hope it doesn't rain,” she whispered.
Papa, whose name was Kamal, packed the rotis. “It might, beta. If it does, we'll eat in the bus and go another Sunday.”
“But it might not.”
“It might not,” Kamal agreed. He set the umbrella beside the bag anyway.
The first drops tapped the glass. Arohi uncrossed her fingers slowly. “Can I still wear my hat?”

qa.q: What time did the picnic bus leave?
qa.a: The picnic bus left at nine.

qa.q: What was Arohi feeling as she whispered with her fingers crossed, and what else might it be?
qa.a: Hopeful: she wanted dry weather and believed it might happen, so she said “But it might not.” Underneath there may be some worry about being disappointed.

qa.q: How did Kamal prepare Arohi for a letdown?
qa.a: He said honestly that it might rain and offered a plan, without crushing her hope, and he still put the umbrella beside the bag.

qa.q: How might Kamal feel watching Arohi at the window?
qa.a: Probably hopeful for her yet a little anxious she will be let down, and he stayed gentle in his words. 🤍

grounding: A child crosses fingers and repeats a hope about rain; honest gentle talk prepares for a letdown.

passage:
In the colony park, Ishita crossed her fingers and squeezed her eyes shut. “I hope it doesn't rain tomorrow. I hope the picnic happens.”
Her friend Pranav, on the next swing, said, “My Mummy says clouds are coming.”
Ishita opened one eye. “But maybe they go away.”
“Maybe.”
Her mother, hanging washing on the balcony above, called down, “Maybe, Ishita. If not, we'll spread the big sheet inside and it will still be a picnic.”
Ishita thought about it. “With sandwiches?”
“With sandwiches.”

qa.q: What did Pranav say his Mummy said was coming?
qa.a: He said clouds were coming.

qa.q: What is Ishita feeling and wanting when she squeezes her eyes shut and crosses her fingers?
qa.a: She is hopeful: she wants the picnic to happen and believes the wish might help. Her question about sandwiches afterwards shows she can begin to accept another plan, though she may also be hiding some disappointment.

qa.q: What would you advise Ishita's mother to do if it does rain?
qa.a: Acknowledge the disappointment first, then bring out the indoor picnic sheet she promised so the day still feels special.

qa.q: How might Pranav see Ishita's wishing?
qa.a: He passes on what his Mummy said, so he may think rain is likely and not want to hurt her feelings, or he may be hoping too.

grounding: A child crosses fingers hoping for no rain; honest gentle talk prepares for a letdown.

passage:
On the veranda of the farmhouse, Kamal held his slate up with both hands. “Look, Amma! A buffalo!” Rukmini wiped her wet hands on her sari and bent down. The buffalo had four uneven legs and one enormous eye. “Ah, you made the horns curl. And the tail swings.”
Kamal's chest puffed out. “I did the tail three times.”
“Three times! You kept trying.”
“Now you do a hen.”
Rukmini laughed. “I will do a very bad hen.” They sat down together on the step.

qa.q: How many times did Kamal do the tail?
qa.a: He said he did the tail three times.

qa.q: How can you tell Kamal felt proud, and what else might it show?
qa.a: His chest puffed out, he held the slate up with both hands and told her about the tail. It might also show he wanted her attention while she was busy.

qa.q: What kind of praise helped here, and why?
qa.a: Rukmini noticed specific effort, the curled horns and the repeated tail, instead of saying “best ever”, so Kamal's pride is tied to his own trying. 🙂

qa.q: What might Rukmini be feeling as she wipes her hands and bends down?
qa.a: Probably warmth and delight, since she stopped what she was doing to look. She might also be busy or tired but chose to give him her attention.

grounding: A preschooler says look with a drawing; pride grows with attention to real effort.

passage:
By the cubbies, Santiago sat on the floor with his sneaker in his lap, tongue between his teeth, looping the lace the way Mr Kofi had shown the group. It took a long time, and the other children were already outside. At last he pulled, and the bow sat slightly crooked on his foot. He jumped up. “Mr Kofi! Look, look!”
Mr Kofi crouched. “You tied it yourself. I watched you work on it.”
“I did the loop and the other loop.”
“You did.”
Santiago grinned. “Now the other one.”

qa.q: Which teacher did Santiago show his shoe to?
qa.a: He showed it to Mr Kofi.

qa.q: What was Santiago feeling when he grinned and asked to do the other shoe?
qa.a: Proud and pleased with his effort, and keen to keep going. He could also simply be enjoying Mr Kofi's attention.

qa.q: What would you advise a teacher to say to a child showing a tied shoe?
qa.a: Notice the real effort, as Mr Kofi did with “I watched you work on it”, and share the delight without heavy praise.

qa.q: How might Mr Kofi see the crooked bow?
qa.a: As the result of Santiago's real work rather than a mistake to fix, since he praised what he watched the boy do and not how neat the bow was.

grounding: A preschooler holds up a tied shoe and says look; shared delight in real effort.

passage:
Saturday: Jeevan trailed behind Rashmi from room to room. “What can I do? There's nothing.” She offered blocks or chalk on the balcony. “No,” he said, and lay down on the floor.
Tuesday: “What can I do?” he asked again, dragging a sock along. Rashmi said, “Here's a big box and some pegs. You pick.” He shrugged and wandered off with the box.
Thursday: the flat was quiet. Jeevan sat in the box with a wooden spoon for a steering wheel. “Mummy, I'm driving to Nani's!” he called, without looking up.

qa.q: What did Jeevan use as a steering wheel?
qa.a: He used a wooden spoon as a steering wheel.

qa.q: What was Jeevan feeling on Saturday when he lay on the floor, and what else might it mean?
qa.a: Most likely bored and restless, since nothing held his attention and he turned down both choices. He might also have been tired or wanted Rashmi's company more than an activity.

qa.q: What small step helps a bored child, judging by this passage?
qa.a: Offering a couple of open choices and then leaving some boredom, as Rashmi did with the box, so he could make up his own game. 🙂

qa.q: How might Rashmi feel on Saturday when he refused both ideas?
qa.a: Perhaps frustrated or unsure, since both were refused. She chose to try something different later instead of giving up, which suggests patience.

grounding: A bored preschooler whines and wanders; choices and some boredom lead to a self-made game.

passage:
The train was two hours late and the platform bench was hard. Chetan had counted the pigeons, the pillars and the tea stalls. “I'm boooored. What can I do?” he whined, swinging his legs.
Leela Nani rummaged in her bag and found a ribbon of string and a small notebook. “You choose: cat's cradle, or write down every colour you see.”
Chetan scowled. “Both are boring.”
Nani said nothing and watched the tracks. After a while he took the notebook and drew a wobbly red shirt on the man near the tea stall. “His shirt is red,” he announced.

qa.q: What had Chetan counted on the platform?
qa.a: He had counted the pigeons, the pillars and the tea stalls.

qa.q: What might Chetan be feeling when he says both are boring, and what else could be behind it?
qa.a: Probably restless and bored with the long wait. The refusal might also come from tiredness or a wish to choose his own thing. He takes the notebook later, so the boredom eased.

qa.q: What could Nani try next if the notebook loses its appeal?
qa.a: Let him choose again, or leave a little quiet so he invents something himself, as happened here.

qa.q: How might Nani feel when he scowls at her ideas?
qa.a: Perhaps a bit tired herself from the delay. She chose to stay quiet rather than argue, which gave him room.

grounding: A bored child wanders and whines on a long wait; offered choices and space, he starts a task of his own.

subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
passage:
Kalyani burst through the door of the fourth-floor flat with her cheeks bright red. Her mother, Ritu, looked up from the pressure cooker. “So red! Were you racing on the stairs?”
“A little.”
“It's warm on the stairs too.”
Kalyani twisted her skirt. “A boy in the lift said my drawing folder looked nice.”
Ritu smiled but did not tease. “Maybe your cheeks are red from running, or shyness, or feeling a bit proud. Which one?”
Kalyani thought. “Little bit all.”
“That's allowed.”

qa.q: What did a boy in the lift say to Kalyani?
qa.a: He said her drawing folder looked nice.

qa.q: What might Kalyani have been feeling when she twisted her skirt, and why can't we be certain?
qa.a: Probably shy and a bit proud about the compliment, but her red cheeks could also come from racing on the stairs and the warmth. She herself said “Little bit all.”

qa.q: How could Ritu's response help Kalyani?
qa.a: By naming several possible feelings gently and not teasing, she gives Kalyani words to use and avoids shame about blushing.

qa.q: What would change if Ritu had laughed at Kalyani's red cheeks?
qa.a: Kalyani might feel embarrassed and hide her feelings next time, even from a kind mother. Blushing would start to feel like something to be ashamed of.

grounding: Red cheeks may come from running, heat, shyness or pride; naming gently helps.

passage:
“Look, tomato cheeks!” said Mohit, pointing. “Divyansh is a tomato!”
“I'm not!” Divyansh pressed both hands to his face and turned to the wall. “Mohit Bhaiya, don't laugh.”
“Mohit, enough,” said Mummy. “Divyansh, come here. You ran three rounds of the courtyard and it's hot. Are your cheeks red from running?”
“And... Mohit was looking.”
“So maybe a little shy too?”
He nodded into her dupatta.
“Mohit, no more teasing about cheeks.”
“Okay, sorry,” said Mohit.

qa.q: How many rounds of the courtyard had Divyansh run?
qa.a: He had run three rounds of the courtyard.

qa.q: Why did Divyansh turn to the wall, and what else could explain his red cheeks?
qa.a: He was probably embarrassed and upset about being teased, since he asked Mohit not to laugh. The redness could also come from running in the heat, so it may not be only shyness.

qa.q: How could Mummy help further?
qa.a: She could ask Divyansh gently how he feels, and let him sit in the shade with some water while he settles.

qa.q: How might Mohit see the teasing?
qa.a: He may think it is harmless fun and not see that Divyansh feels embarrassed. When Mummy stops him, he may start to understand.

grounding: Red cheeks may come from running, heat or shyness; teasing raises shame while naming gently helps.
